scope: Publisher-rendered telescope images and explicitly identified inferred overlays. No image pixels are fitted or used to initialize the test-particle simulation. Sky references are publisher image centres except Bullet Cluster, for which the publisher object reference is retained; none are measured 3D positions.

targets.title: Inside the Great Attractor region
targets.question: Which galaxies trace the local pull?
targets.context: The Norma Cluster lies in the Great Attractor region, behind a crowded foreground of Milky Way stars. It is one part of a larger gravitational environment, not a destination toward which every galaxy in the universe is falling.
targets.observed: Galaxies and foreground stars emit the light in these images. Dust in our own galaxy obscures some of the background. The narrow Hubble field includes the edge-on galaxy ESO 137-002.
targets.inferred: A cluster's gravitational influence depends on its total mass and surroundings. A photograph alone does not give its mass, a galaxy's independent distance or its peculiar velocity.
targets.next: Match galaxy identities to spectroscopy and independent distance indicators. Fit line-of-sight velocities with distance errors, survey selection and calibration covariance before testing local versus distant attraction.
targets.comparison: These are different pointings, orientations and fields of view. Switching images is a context comparison, not a registered overlay or a time sequence.

layers.label: Hubble · galaxy detail
layers.alt: Hubble view of the Norma Cluster field, with an edge-on galaxy and many bright foreground stars.
layers.interpretation: Light from galaxies and stars. Their apparent size and brightness do not directly specify their distance or motion.

layers.label: ESO · wider environment
layers.bands: B, R and 816 nm; assigned colours and logarithmic intensity
layers.alt: Wide-field ESO image toward the Norma Cluster, with a dense foreground star field and background galaxies.
layers.interpretation: A much larger patch of sky reveals the crowded observing conditions. The brightest points can be foreground stars rather than cluster members.

targets.title: A cluster acting as a lens
targets.question: What can distorted background galaxies tell us?
targets.context: Abell 2744 is a distant merging cluster at redshift z = 0.308. It is a comparison system for studying mass through lensing, not a component of the nearby Great Attractor model.
targets.observed: Hubble and Webb record light in different wavelength bands. Some stretched images are background galaxies whose light has been deflected by foreground mass.
targets.inferred: A gravitational-lens model uses image positions, source redshifts and other constraints to estimate projected mass. A visible arc is evidence to model, not a direct image of dark matter.
targets.next: Use calibrated exposures, astrometry, multiple-image identifications, spectroscopic redshifts and ensembles of lens models. Compare uncertainties rather than estimating mass from a colour JPEG.
targets.comparison: Hubble and Webb views differ in pointing, orientation, coverage, filters and processing. They are not pixel-aligned; apparent colour differences are not evidence for motion or physical change.

layers.label: JWST · infrared
layers.credit: NASA, ESA, CSA, I. Labbe (Swinburne University of Technology), R. Bezanson (University of Pittsburgh), A. Pagan (STScI)
layers.alt: Webb infrared view of Abell 2744 with bright cluster galaxies, many faint background galaxies and gravitationally stretched arcs.
layers.interpretation: Near-infrared light rendered in visible colours. This layer contains no added dark-matter mass contours.

layers.label: Hubble · optical + infrared
layers.credit: NASA, ESA, and J. Lotz, M. Mountain, A. Koekemoer, and the HFF Team (STScI).
layers.alt: Hubble Frontier Fields image of Abell 2744, showing cluster galaxies and elongated background images.
layers.interpretation: Optical and near-infrared light. The narrower field is shown in full; its displayed size is not the same angular scale as the Webb view.

targets.title: Where the light and mass separate
targets.question: Does the gravitating mass follow the hot gas?
targets.context: Two distant galaxy clusters are colliding. Their gas and galaxies respond differently to the encounter. This system is a test of matter physics, not a photograph of the Great Attractor.
targets.observed: Webb detects near-infrared starlight. Chandra detects X-rays from hot gas, displayed in pink. Switch between the publisher's layers to see which structures emit in each band.
targets.inferred: The blue component of the composite is a lensing-derived mass distribution. Its separation from the gas supports a substantial dark-matter component under the gravitational model used; the blue colour is not detected dark-matter light.
targets.next: A quantitative offset or dark-matter-interaction test needs calibrated images, a lensing mass posterior, gas-centroid errors and merger geometry. The rendered blue overlay cannot supply those uncertainties.
targets.comparison: These layers come from the same 2025 publisher image set, but the standalone X-ray JPEG has a different crop and aspect ratio. No new registration is applied. Do not measure offsets between these displayed frames; they are not a collision movie.

layers.interpretation: Pink = observed hot-gas emission. Blue = inferred mass. The overlay is the publisher's scientific interpretation, not an additional telescope wavelength.

layers.field: Standalone crop differs; angular extent not verified for this JPEG

targets.title: A distance indicator, not a dark-energy photo
targets.question: How does light become evidence for expansion?
targets.context: A Type Ia supernova can be standardized using its light curve and colour. Comparing many calibrated distances with redshifts tests the expansion history. One photograph cannot establish cosmic acceleration.
targets.observed: Hubble resolves the host galaxy and the bright supernova. Photometric measurements over time, rather than this display image, are used to construct a light curve.
targets.inferred: Standardized supernova luminosities provide distance estimates. Cosmological fits to a population constrain expansion; dark energy is an interpretation of accelerated expansion, not a luminous component in this image.
targets.next: The expansion lab already fits the pinned Pantheon+ / SH0ES table and covariance. This photograph illustrates the method; no catalog identity join or pixel-level fit for SN 1994D is made here.
targets.comparison: The release date below is the image's publication date, not a supernova explosion date. This is a single observational view, not a time series.

layers.label: Hubble · SN 1994D
layers.bands: Publisher colour image; see original release
layers.credit: NASA/ESA, The Hubble Key Project Team and The High-Z Supernova Search Team
layers.alt: Hubble image of NGC 4526 with its dark dust lane and the bright point of supernova SN 1994D beside the galaxy.
layers.interpretation: Observed starlight, dust absorption and a supernova. There is no dark-energy overlay because dark energy has not been photographed.
